assessments.reasoning: GNU’s fdl-1.1.txt identifies the March 2000 edition. Bytes [2781,2968) define Cover Texts by their listing in the work notice. Bytes [5354,6310) supply the printed-copy trigger, front/back assignment, legibility requirement and overflow advice. The broader medium language in later editions is absent here.

challenge.method: Compare 100 and 101 printed copies with the same required texts. Then remove the texts from the notice, change to a nonprinted medium that commonly has printed covers, and overload one cover.
challenge.results: Exactly 100 falls outside the rule. At 101 printed copies the rule applies if the notice requires texts. A notice requiring none defeats that trigger. A nonprinted medium’s customary printed cover does not bring it within the 1.1 wording. When one cover cannot fit all its texts legibly, the publisher should start with the first-listed texts that reasonably fit there and continue the rest on adjacent pages. Overflow supplies no basis to omit the remainder.

limitations: The actual work’s authorized notice identifies its Cover Texts. The GNU license file alone establishes none for a particular work.
The claim addresses placement. Section 3 also addresses publisher identification, title presentation and, under a separate trigger, Opaque copies.
reasoning: GNU FDL 1.1 §3 makes legible placement of the designated front and back texts mandatory when a publisher issues more than 100 printed copies and the Document’s license notice requires those texts. The next paragraph uses advisory language for the particular way of handling overflow on either cover.
